sense: the tool or the part of the body used

terms.grammar: construction: the tool in the ablative, with no preposition
evidence: Cato Agr. 45.1: malleō aut mateolā adigitō
Varr. RR 1.55.2: harundine potius quam perticā feriantur
terms.comment: Latin does not use cum with a tool: cultrō secāre, to cut with a knife; manū tangere, to touch with the hand. Cum with a thing means having it along (see “with”, in company).

terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, deponent, with the ablative
terms.comment: For “with” meaning “using”: ūtere furcillā, use your fork.

phrases.latin: cum tāleam dēmittēs, pede tāleam opprimitō. sī parum dēscendet, malleō aut mateolā adigitō
phrases.english: when you set the cutting, press it down with your foot; if it doesn’t go deep enough, drive it in with a hammer or a mallet

phrases.latin: quae manū tangī nōn poterunt, ita quatī dēbent, ut harundine potius quam perticā feriantur; gravior enim plāga medicum quaerit
phrases.english: the ones that can’t be reached by hand should be knocked down with a reed rather than a pole; a heavier blow calls for a doctor

phrases.latin: manibus siccīs, cum ūtī volēs, sūmitō
phrases.english: when you want to use them, take them out with dry hands

phrases.latin: pōnētur digitīs tenendus ūnctīs nigrā cōliculus virēns patellā
phrases.english: a green cabbage sprout will be served on a black dish, to be held in oily fingers

phrases.latin: cum autem paulum firmitātis accessit, et animō ūtuntur et sēnsibus cōnītunturque, ut sēsē ērigant, et manibus ūtuntur et eōs agnōscunt, ā quibus ēducantur
phrases.english: when they have grown a little stronger, babies use their minds and senses, try to stand up, use their hands, and know the people who bring them up

sources: Lewis & Short: ablativus · Lewis & Short: utor · Lewis & Short: cum
